title: 25 Jun 2018
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall, 25 June 2018 (a candidate who passed with 85% noted that about half the questions were repeats). Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: Which antibody test is most specific for diagnosing systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: ANA is the best screening test (very sensitive), while anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific; anti-dsDNA and complement follow activity, especially lupus nephritis.

questions.question: A child who has had a stem cell transplant is exposed to his brother's chickenpox. What should be given?
questions.exp: Immunocompromised children exposed to varicella need VZIG within 10 days (or oral aciclovir from day 7 to 14), and IV aciclovir if chickenpox develops. Live vaccines are contraindicated.

questions.question: A child has a ring-shaped skin lesion that is not scaly and does not respond to antifungal cream. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Granuloma annulare: skin-coloured or pink papules in an annular ring, without scale, often on the backs of the hands and feet; it resolves over months to years. Tinea is scaly with an active border and responds to antifungals.

questions.question: A child has a metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia and a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hyperchloraemic acidosis with low potassium and an inappropriately high urine pH (over 5.5) is distal RTA; it causes nephrocalcinosis and poor growth. Treat with oral alkali.

questions.question: Which vaccine is given intradermally?
questions.exp: BCG is given intradermally into the left upper arm (deltoid insertion); MMR and varicella are subcutaneous; inactivated vaccines are intramuscular.

questions.question: A child has a hot, swollen, painful knee with fever. What is the key step?
questions.a: Joint aspiration for Gram stain and culture, then IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Septic arthritis: aspirate (usually with washout in theatre), take blood cultures, then start IV antibiotics covering Staph aureus and Kingella (such as cefazolin, or clindamycin where MRSA is common).

questions.question: What BMI defines obesity in a child?
questions.a: At or above the 95th centile for age and sex
questions.exp: In children, BMI centiles are used: overweight 85th–94th centile, obese at or above the 95th centile (US CDC). UK clinical cut-offs use the 91st (overweight) and 98th (obese) centiles.

questions.question: What is the first-line antibiotic for acute otitis media when one is needed?
questions.exp: Most AOM resolves in 3 days without antibiotics. Give antibiotics for children under 2 with bilateral AOM, otorrhoea, systemic illness or no improvement: amoxicillin first-line (co-amoxiclav if recent amoxicillin), clarithromycin if penicillin allergic.

questions.question: A child has liver disease, neurological signs and Kayser–Fleischer rings. Which test supports the diagnosis?
questions.b: Low serum caeruloplasmin (with high urinary copper)
questions.exp: Wilson disease: low caeruloplasmin, high 24-hour urine copper (rising after penicillamine challenge), Kayser–Fleischer rings, high liver copper. Treat with chelation (penicillamine or trientine) and zinc.

questions.question: What is the sodium content of 0.45% sodium chloride?
questions.exp: 0.45% saline contains half the sodium of 0.9% (154 mmol/L). Isotonic fluids are now preferred for maintenance to avoid hyponatraemia.

questions.question: A child with seizures has a port-wine stain on the face since birth. Which finding supports the diagnosis of Sturge–Weber syndrome?
questions.exp: Sturge–Weber: facial port-wine stain (V1), leptomeningeal angioma with tram-track calcification, seizures, hemiparesis and glaucoma.

questions.question: How is mid-parental height calculated for a girl?
questions.exp: For girls subtract 13 cm from the father's height before averaging; for boys add 13 cm to the mother's height.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has cataracts, learning disability, rickets and a renal tubular problem (Fanconi syndrome). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lowe syndrome (OCRL, X-linked): congenital cataracts, hypotonia, intellectual disability and renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets. Cystinosis gives Fanconi syndrome with corneal crystals but not cataracts at birth.

questions.question: A neonate has bilious vomiting and has not passed stool. The X-ray shows a double bubble. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Double bubble (stomach and proximal duodenum) with no distal gas is duodenal atresia (with Down syndrome in about 30%); bilious if the block is below the ampulla. Gastric decompression and duodenoduodenostomy.

questions.question: A child arrives with a heart rate of 40/min and respiratory rate of 20, and is poorly responsive. What is the underlying problem?
questions.exp: In children, bradycardia is usually a pre-terminal sign of hypoxia; a poorly responsive child with bradycardia and inadequate breathing needs oxygen, ventilation, and CPR if the heart rate is under 60 with poor perfusion.

questions.question: A child due for vaccines has a red tympanic membrane from mild otitis media and a low-grade fever. What should be done?
questions.exp: Minor illnesses without high fever (colds, otitis media, mild diarrhoea) are not contraindications to vaccination; only postpone for an acute moderate or severe illness.

questions.question: A bottle-fed infant who was previously well has focal seizures on the right side. What clinical finding is most likely?
questions.exp: Seizures in an infant without fever or metabolic cause can be due to abusive head trauma; look for retinal haemorrhages, bruising and fractures, and get a CT/MRI brain.

questions.question: A 9-month-old weighing 5 kg has a VSD with a loud second heart sound (pulmonary hypertension) and poor weight gain despite captopril and furosemide. What should be done?
questions.a: Continue medicines and review at 2 years
questions.b: Pulmonary artery banding only at 5 years
questions.exp: A VSD causing heart failure, failure to thrive or pulmonary hypertension despite medical treatment needs surgical closure, ideally before 6–12 months, to prevent irreversible pulmonary vascular disease.

questions.question: Which is NOT a feature of vitamin D toxicity?
questions.exp: Hypervitaminosis D causes hypercalcaemia: vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, polyuria, polydipsia, irritability, nephrocalcinosis and renal failure.

questions.question: Which milk has the best absorbed iron for infants?
questions.exp: Breast milk contains little iron, but about 50% is absorbed, compared with about 10% from cow's milk and formula; formula is fortified to compensate. Exclusively breastfed term infants need iron-rich weaning foods from 6 months.

questions.question: Which deficiency can cause pancytopenia?
questions.exp: Severe megaloblastic anaemia can lower all three cell lines (ineffective haematopoiesis), with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils; exclude leukaemia and aplastic anaemia.

questions.question: A child drank kerosene and has mild tachypnoea. What is the first treatment?
questions.a: Oxygen and observation (no vomiting, lavage or charcoal)
questions.exp: Hydrocarbon aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis; treat with oxygen and supportive care, and a chest X-ray at about 6 hours.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy has mild bilateral breast enlargement during puberty. What should be done?
questions.a: Reassure; pubertal gynaecomastia usually settles within 1–2 years
questions.exp: Physiological pubertal gynaecomastia affects up to 2 in 3 boys and resolves in most. Investigate if large, with small testes (Klinefelter), drugs or anabolic steroid use, or signs of tumours.

questions.question: What is the antidote to paracetamol poisoning?
questions.exp: NAC replenishes glutathione; it is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion but is given to any patient at risk of liver injury.

questions.question: A teenager has comedones and inflamed pustules on the face. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.c: Topical benzoyl peroxide (with a topical retinoid)
questions.exp: Mild to moderate acne: topical benzoyl peroxide and retinoids, adding topical or oral antibiotics for inflammatory lesions.

questions.question: A febrile child (38°C) has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure lasting more than 30 minutes. What is the classification?
questions.b: Status epilepticus (febrile status), needing assessment for CNS infection
questions.exp: A seizure over 30 minutes (operationally over 5 minutes) is status epilepticus; fever with prolonged seizures needs evaluation for meningitis or encephalitis, especially in young infants.

questions.question: A mother had an intrauterine fetal death from hydrops. Which test helps diagnose fetomaternal haemorrhage as the cause?
questions.a: Kleihauer–Betke test on the mother's blood
questions.d: Direct Coombs test on the baby
questions.exp: The Kleihauer test detects fetal red cells in the mother's circulation and quantifies the bleed; also check maternal antibodies (alloimmunisation), infections (parvovirus) and others in hydrops.

questions.question: A baby had diarrhoea and vomiting, then dark urine and purpura. What is the cause of the purpura?
questions.exp: Diarrhoea followed by haemolysis, low platelets and kidney injury is typical HUS.

questions.question: At a routine check, a mother says her 2-week-old has a blocked nose but feeds well. What should she be told?
questions.c: It is normal; newborns are nose breathers and often have nasal congestion
questions.exp: Physiological neonatal nasal congestion is common and settles; saline drops can help. Refer if there is respiratory distress, cyanosis relieved by crying (choanal atresia), or feeding problems.

questions.question: A 2-year-old says 10 words, walks alone and draws a line. What is the advice?
questions.b: Language is delayed for his age; arrange a hearing test and speech and language assessment
questions.exp: By 2 years most children use 50 or more words and combine 2 words. Fewer than 50 words or no word combinations at 2 years warrants a hearing test and speech assessment, and screening for autism.

questions.question: A boy can copy a triangle, dress himself and tidy his clothes away. What is his age?
questions.exp: Copying a triangle and dressing fully (except laces) are expected at 5 years; a square at 4 years; a diamond at 6.

questions.question: Which chemotherapy drug commonly causes pancreatitis?
questions.exp: Asparaginase (used in ALL) can cause pancreatitis, thrombosis, hyperglycaemia and allergic reactions; check amylase or lipase with abdominal pain. Valproate and steroids are other drug causes.

questions.question: A 4-year-old is restless and irritable, and the ECG shows peaked T waves. What is the immediate management?
questions.exp: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin–glucose and salbutamol to shift K+, and resins or dialysis to remove it.

questions.question: An infant has tachypnoea, a heart rate of 220/min with a narrow QRS, and a liver 5 cm below the costal margin. What is the treatment?
questions.c: Adenosine (after vagal manoeuvres, or synchronised cardioversion if shocked)
questions.exp: SVT with heart failure: adenosine if stable enough and access is available; synchronised DC cardioversion if shocked. Prolonged SVT in infants often presents with heart failure.

questions.question: A 2-day-old has delayed passage of meconium and the X-ray suggests Hirschsprung disease. What is the next step to confirm it?
questions.exp: Rectal suction biopsy (absent ganglion cells) is the gold standard; a contrast enema shows the transition zone and helps plan surgery.

questions.question: Which features define autism spectrum disorder?
questions.b: Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, with restricted, repetitive behaviours or interests, starting in early childhood
questions.exp: DSM-5 criteria: social communication and interaction deficits, and restricted repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (including sensory differences), present from early development and causing impairment.
